questions.question: Physicians are reluctant to prescribe beta-lactam antibiotics to patients with a documented penicillin allergy on their chart.
questions.question_raw: 23. Physicians are reluctant to prescribe beta-lactam antibiotics to patients with a documented penicillin allergy on their chart.

parts.text: What are four clinical markers of a Type I / IgE-mediated reaction?
What is the antigenic component of cross-reactivity between penicillin and cephalosporin?
If the patient had a Stevens-Johnson reaction to penicillin in the past, can you use penicillin again? Under what circumstances?

parts_raw.text: What are four clinical markers of a Type I / IgE-mediated reaction? (2)
What is antigenic component of cross-reactivity between penicillin and cephalosporin? (1)
If the patient had a Stevens-Johnsons reaction to penicillin in the past, can you use penicillin again? Under what circumstances? (1)

questions.model_answer: a) Immediate/accelerated onset (<1 hour after administration): (1) pruritus, (2) urticaria/angioedema, (3) bronchospasm, (4) anaphylaxis (hypotension). b) The R1 side chain — cross-reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins is predicted by shared R1 side chains (e.g., ampicillin/amoxicillin with cephalexin/cefadroxil), not the core beta-lactam ring. c) No. SJS (a severe cutaneous adverse reaction) is a contraindication to penicillin re-exposure: penicillin skin testing/challenge has no value and desensitization is contraindicated in SJS/TEN. The patient is not a candidate for penicillin re-exposure under any circumstance; use a carbapenem or aztreonam instead.
questions.cohort_conflict: The cohort suggests rechallenge via incremental drug challenge with monitoring if disease is severe and no alternatives exist; Mandell states penicillin skin testing/challenge has no value in SJS/TEN and that such patients are not candidates for re-exposure (use carbapenem or aztreonam), so re-exposure should be avoided.

cohort_answer.text: Markers: immediate or accelerated onset (30 min-1 hr, rarely 6-48hrs), pruritus and urticaria, bronchospasm, anaphylaxis. Cross-reactivity component: R1 side chain. SJS history: avoid use of any beta-lactams in a patient with history of SJS/TEN/severe cutaneous adverse reactions to another beta-lactam; severe disease and lack of alternatives may warrant rechallenge via carefully designed incremental drug challenge with frequent monitoring

questions.model_answer: a) Selective aminopenicillin allergy: the reaction is directed at the R1 (aminobenzyl) side chain of ampicillin rather than the core beta-lactam determinant, so the patient reacts to the aminopenicillin but tolerates penicillin. b) Avoid amoxicillin — it shares the same aminobenzyl R1 side chain as ampicillin.

cohort_answer.text: Reason: Different R1 side chain, still high risk for cross reaction but not 100%. Avoid: Avoid amoxicillin (almost the same)

questions.question: β-Lactams.

parts.text: Mechanism of action?
What is the main pharmacodynamic parameter that affects the action of the drug?
Given this, what is a way to administer the drug that would make it more effective?
What percentage of patients who say they have a penicillin allergy have a positive skin test?

parts_raw.text: Mechanism of action?
What's the main pharmacodynamic parameter that affects the action of the drug?
Given this, what is a way to administer the drug that would make it more effective?
What percentage of patients who say they have a penicillin allergy have a positive skin test?

questions.model_answer:
a) β-Lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) and irreversibly inhibit their transpeptidase/transglycosylase activity, blocking cross-linking of the peptidoglycan cell wall; the slow deacylation of the penicillin-bound PBP amounts to irreversible enzyme inhibition, arresting cell-wall synthesis and producing bactericidal killing.
b) Time-dependent killing: the fraction of the dosing interval that free drug concentration remains above the MIC (fT>MIC).
c) Maximize time above MIC by giving more frequent doses, or by prolonged/extended or continuous infusion rather than short bolus dosing.
d) Only a minority: roughly 10% or fewer of patients reporting a penicillin allergy have a positive skin test (correspondingly, >90% test negative), and <2% of those with a reported history react when challenged.
questions.beyond_mandell: The time-above-MIC PD parameter and continuous/extended-infusion strategy are established antimicrobial pharmacodynamics, not stated in this chapter slice; the skin-test-positive percentage is standard allergy teaching (the chapter states <2% react on challenge).

questions.question: A patient recently had a Type 1 hypersensitivity reaction to ampicillin. Skin testing with major and minor determinants was negative and an oral challenge with penicillin was also negative.
questions.question_raw: 19) Pt recently had Type 1 hypersensitivity reaction to ampicillin. A skin test is done with major and minor determinants, which is negative. An oral challenge with Penicillin is also negative.

parts.text: What is the most likely explanation for this?
What is one other drug you should counsel this patient to avoid, other than amoxicillin?

parts_raw.text: What is the most likely explanation for this?
What is one other drug you should counsel this patient to avoid, other than amoxicillin?

questions.model_answer: a) Selective aminopenicillin allergy directed at the R1 (aminobenzyl) side chain of ampicillin rather than the core penicillin determinant, so penicillin determinant testing and penicillin challenge are negative. b) Cephalexin (or cefadroxil, or cefaclor) — these share the aminobenzyl R1 side chain of ampicillin/amoxicillin and predict cross-reactivity.

cohort_answer.text: Ampicillin had a different R1-side chain from penicillin. Ampicillin has a side chain identical to that of first-generation cephalosporins cephalexin and cefadroxil, and to cefaclor (2nd gen cephalosporin) - avoid these (NOT cefazolin).

questions.model_answer:
a) They bind PBPs and inhibit the transpeptidase-mediated cross-linking of peptidoglycan; the slowly reversible acyl-enzyme complex irreversibly inhibits the PBP, halting cell-wall synthesis and killing the organism.
b) Time-dependent killing - the percentage of the dosing interval that free drug stays above the MIC (fT>MIC).
c) Prolonged, extended, or continuous infusion (and/or more frequent dosing) to maximize time above MIC.
d) More than 90% will have a negative skin test (the great majority of reported penicillin allergies are not confirmed).
questions.beyond_mandell: T>MIC and continuous/extended infusion are established PD principles not in this slice; the >90% negative-skin-test figure is standard penicillin-allergy teaching.

parts_raw.text: What are FOUR symptoms/manifestations of IgE mediated allergic reaction?
What is the antigenic component that causes cross-reactivity between beta-lactams?
If your patient had a previous history of SJS/TENs with penicillin, would you prescribe a cephalosporin? If so, under what circumstances?

questions.model_answer: a) Immediate (<1 hour) IgE-mediated manifestations: (1) pruritus, (2) urticaria/angioedema, (3) bronchospasm, (4) anaphylaxis (hypotension). b) The R1 side chain — cross-reactivity among beta-lactams is based on R1 side-chain similarity rather than the shared beta-lactam ring. c) No. With a history of SJS/TEN (a severe cutaneous adverse reaction) to penicillin, cephalosporins should not be used under any circumstance; the patient is not a candidate for penicillins or cephalosporins. Use a carbapenem or aztreonam instead.

questions.model_answer:
a) Penicillin binds PBPs and inhibits transpeptidase cross-linking of peptidoglycan; the stable acyl-enzyme complex irreversibly inactivates the PBP, arresting cell-wall synthesis and killing dividing bacteria.
b) Time-dependent killing - free concentration above the MIC for a sufficient fraction of the dosing interval (fT>MIC).
c) Optimize the dose/interval to maximize time above MIC, e.g. more frequent dosing or prolonged/continuous infusion.
d) More than 90% of patients reporting a penicillin allergy have a negative skin test.
questions.beyond_mandell: T>MIC, infusion optimization, and the >90% negative-skin-test figure are established teaching, not detailed in this slice.

cohort_answer.text: a) Binds PBP and prevents cross-linking of cell wall. b) Time over MIC dependent (t/MIC). c) Optimize dose such that time above MIC is optimized. d) >90%.

questions.model_answer: a) Posaconazole: lanosterol 14-alpha-demethylase (Erg11/CYP51), blocking conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol. b) Micafungin: 1,3-beta-D-glucan synthase (fungal cell wall synthesis). c) Amphotericin: ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane — the polyene binds ergosterol, forming pores that increase membrane permeability. d) Terbinafine: squalene epoxidase (squalene monooxygenase), an early step in ergosterol biosynthesis.

questions.question: A pregnant woman is admitted with mild community-acquired pneumonia and has a history of Stevens-Johnson syndrome to penicillin. What is your treatment?
questions.question_raw: Pneumonia (inpatient, mild) in a pregnant woman with SJ to PCN.

parts.text: What is your treatment?

parts_raw.text: What is your treatment.

questions.model_answer: Avoid ALL beta-lactams (including cephalosporins and carbapenems) given the Stevens-Johnson reaction. Give a macrolide, azithromycin (safe in pregnancy, covers atypicals and many pneumococci), combined with clindamycin for typical gram-positive (S. pneumoniae, S. aureus) coverage; add aztreonam if gram-negative coverage is required. Avoid fluoroquinolones and doxycycline in pregnancy if alternatives exist.
questions.beyond_mandell: Chapter gives the beta-lactam-allergy ICU regimen (respiratory fluoroquinolone +/- clindamycin) but not pregnancy-specific choices; regimen based on CAP guidance plus pregnancy safety (macrolides safe, quinolones/doxycycline avoided).

cohort_answer.text: Macrolides are safe for pregnancy. UpToDate suggests: Clindamycin plus aztreonam for mild CAP requiring admission with contraindication to cephalosporins. Short course of Moxifloxacin should be fine (author's opinion). If severe: Vancomycin, aztreonam and azithromycin. (ATS 2001; note - avoid all beta-lactams if Stevens-Johnson syndrome.)

questions.question: A pregnant patient has had Stevens-Johnson syndrome to penicillin and is now hospitalized (but not requiring the ICU) with a severe skin/soft tissue infection such as sepsis or necrotizing fasciitis. What empiric antibiotic regimen do you recommend?
questions.question_raw: A pregnant patient has SJS to penicillin. She now is hospitalized, but does not require the ICU. What empiric antibiotic regimen do you recommend? – hospitalized with what…? Use sepsis or nec fasc as an example

parts.text: What empiric antibiotic regimen do you recommend?

parts_raw.text: What empiric antibiotic regimen do you recommend?

questions.model_answer: a) Because SJS is a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction, avoid all beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems). Cover gram-positives (including MRSA/MSSA and streptococci), gram-negatives, and anaerobes, with toxin suppression: (1) Vancomycin IV (MRSA/streptococcal/staphylococcal coverage, replacing the beta-lactam Mandell would otherwise use); (2) Aztreonam IV (gram-negative coverage in place of a beta-lactam); (3) add Clindamycin IV for anaerobic coverage and to suppress streptococcal/staphylococcal toxin production. Urgent surgical exploration/debridement is essential if necrotizing fasciitis is suspected.
questions.beyond_mandell: Aztreonam (a monobactam) is the standard gram-negative substitute for a severe beta-lactam-allergic patient (IDSA SSTI guidance); Mandell's listed necrotizing-fasciitis regimens (piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem plus vancomycin, with clindamycin added for toxin) are all beta-lactam-based and unsuitable here.
